summary: This work demonstrates emission, transmission, and absorption of microwave photons shaped into three mutually orthogonal temporal modes across a 30-meter cryogenic waveguide connecting two superconducting qubits. The orthogonality of these modes enables mode-selective absorption at the receiver, achieving a selectivity ratio of 40 dB between diagonal and off-diagonal transfer matrix elements.
motivation: Conventional quantum communication protocols using symmetric photon envelopes exploit only one temporal degree of freedom; extending to orthogonal temporal modes could enable new applications in waveguide QED such as mode-selective routing, photonic qubit encoding for photon-loss detection, and in-situ channel tomography.
method: Transmon qubits coupled to transfer resonators at rates $\kappa_A = 26.7$ MHz and $\kappa_B = 30.7$ MHz generate photons with envelopes $f_n(t)$ ($n = 0, 1, 2$) via time-dependent f0-g1 drives derived from Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization. The emitter qubit population is tracked during emission to characterize mode shapes; the receiver performs mode-selective absorption by time-reversal of the generation process with matching or mismatched temporal mode.
result: Transfer efficiencies exceed 75% for matched modes ($n_A = n_B$) with delays around $\tau_0 = 145.9 \pm 0.2$ ns consistent with $v_g \approx 0.72c$ in the 30-m waveguide, while mismatched modes ($n_A \neq n_B$) yield receiver $|f\rangle$-state populations of 1–4%, demonstrating orthogonality with a measured selectivity ratio $\Sigma \approx 40 \approx 16$ dB averaged across the $3 \times 3$ mode combination matrix, with 17% photon loss attributed to interface impedance mismatches and control errors.
